overview: The file brings together State Department material on Japanese transportation and military mobility between 1940 and 1942. It includes an October 1941 intelligence radiogram reporting new airfields and Japanese aircraft deployments in French Indochina, a cross-reference to information about supposed Japanese landing fields in Peru, and a March 1940 memorandum on Japan’s effort to achieve automotive self-sufficiency through Nissan and Toyoda while restricting Ford and General Motors. Collectively, the documents connect aviation intelligence, suspected overseas infrastructure, wartime industrial policy, and pressure on American-owned businesses.

subfiles.title: Radiogram on new airfields and Japanese aircraft in French Indochina
subfiles.to: War Department and listed U.S. defense and intelligence offices
subfiles.about: Reports two new airfields and the disposition of seventy-four Japanese military aircraft in French Indochina.
subfiles.summary: British radiogram reports new Indochina airfields and 74 Japanese fighter and bomber aircraft at Hanoi, Tourane, and Saigon, filed October 1941.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to alleged Japanese landing fields in Peru
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a letter concerning supposed Japanese landing fields under construction in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a 1942 Justice Department letter on alleged Japanese landing fields being built in Peru.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s automobile industry and pressure on Ford
subfiles.to: Mr. Hollingsch, according to an OCR-uncertain routing stamp
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese truck production, restrictions on American automobile companies, and negotiations for a Ford-Nissan-Toyoda enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Boyce's report: Nissan and Toyoda each produce about 15,000 army-backed trucks yearly, copied from American models; Japan curtailed Ford and GM import permits, pressuring a reorganization giving Ford 40% and Nissan/Toyoda 30% each in a new company.

interest: Shows 1941 Japanese air-strength intelligence in Indochina, alleged Peru airfields, and Japan's automobile independence drive against Ford.
